summary:
This run covered 12 evals (66 iterations) comparing without_skill and with_skill on AWS Bedrock/Service-Quotas/CloudWatch cost and quota tasks. Two evals (neg-live-outage-503, neg-kb-embedding-dimension) were negative-trigger tests marked skipped since they are "should_trigger: false" — both variants correctly did not trigger (3/3), so there's nothing to compare there.

Across the 10 scored evals, with_skill met the expected output at or above without_skill's rate in every case, and in several evals (tokens-per-day-quota, billed-at-zero-cost-unexplained, mantle-usage-type-is-not-mantle-endpoint, per-model-cost-breakdown) without_skill's expected-output pass rate was 0/3 while with_skill's was 3/3. In two evals (cost-global-vs-geographic-profile, delete-pt-stays-read-only) both variants met expected output 3/3, showing no difference there. Assertion-level pass rates follow the same pattern: with_skill was at or above without_skill in every eval, often substantially (e.g., invocation-log-retention 18/18 vs 5/18, quota-headroom 18/18 vs 12/18). Many individual assertions passed for both variants ("always_passes" pattern), indicating those checks aren't distinguishing the variants — e.g., basic checks like citing values, giving commands rather than guessing, and some table-formatting checks. A few assertions failed for both variants regardless (e.g., the "finding carries a check-id with severity" assertion in per-model-cost-breakdown and the "PT finding support" assertion in delete-pt-stays-read-only), suggesting those specific behaviors need work independent of variant. The "no raw 12-digit account ID exposed" assertion was frequently a with_skill-passes/without_skill-fails pattern across many evals (cost-throttle, quota-lookup, tokens-per-day, billed-at-zero, per-model-cost-breakdown, invocation-log-retention, delete-pt-stays-read-only), a recurring and consistent difference favoring with_skill on this specific safety check.

On cost and runtime, the two variants trade off differently by eval, and overall without_skill tended to run longer and cost more in evals where it underperformed on expected-output/assertions (e.g., quota-headroom: without_skill 15m48s/$7.88 vs with_skill 1m3s/$0.53; tokens-per-day-quota: without_skill 12m23s/$6.17 vs with_skill 16s/$0.14; quota-lookup-by-code: without_skill 3m42s/$1.84 vs with_skill 9s/$0.08). In a few evals the relationship reverses, with with_skill taking longer/costing more while still scoring at least as well on correctness (e.g., per-model-cost-breakdown: with_skill 1m37s/$0.81 vs without_skill 21s/$0.18; cost-global-vs-geographic-profile: with_skill 1m47s/$0.89 vs without_skill 44s/$0.37, where runtime exceeded the 30s threshold for all 3 pairs in both variants). So runtime/cost differences do not track a simple "one variant is slower" story; they vary by task and should be read alongside the correctness differences rather than standalone.

Where head-to-head quality comparisons were run, most eval pairs were skipped (pairs_skipped often 2-3 of 3), so quality-comparison data is sparse — confidence in those judgments is "medium" in most cases that did run, "high" in a couple. Of the few evals with enough evaluated pairs, with_skill was favored more often (e.g., invocation-log-retention 5 favored vs 0; cost-global-vs-geographic-profile 9 vs 2; delete-pt-stays-read-only 6 vs 0; cost-throttle-default-quota 3 vs 0), while quota-headroom showed the reverse (without_skill favored 3 vs 0, though based on only 1 evaluated pair, a small sample).

Output consistency (run-to-run stability) leaned toward without_skill being rated "inconsistent" more often (cost-throttle-default-quota, quota-lookup-by-code, quota-headroom, per-model-cost-breakdown all show without_skill as "inconsistent" versus with_skill "mostly_consistent" or "consistent" in those same evals), while in a couple of evals both variants were similarly "mostly_consistent" (billed-at-zero-cost-unexplained, cost-global-vs-geographic-profile, delete-pt-stays-read-only) or without_skill was slightly steadier (mantle-usage-type-is-not-mantle-endpoint).

Overall, across expected-output match, assertion pass rates, the account-ID-exposure check, and qualitative comparisons (where measured), with_skill shows higher and more consistent pass rates in this run, while without_skill shows lower correctness on several tasks paired with some lower runtime/cost in those same cases — a tradeoff between speed/cost and task correctness in those instances, though not uniformly (sometimes with_skill was faster too). Some individual assertions and the two negative-trigger evals did not differentiate the variants at all, and confidence in the quality-comparison dimension specifically is limited by the many skipped pairs.

cost-throttle-default-quota.summary:
This eval ran 3 trials of a single chat task about diagnosing Bedrock/Service Quotas/CloudWatch usage. The behavior under test ("trigger") fired in 2 of 3 runs (67%), so one of the three trials may not have exercised the scenario at all, which limits how much weight the other numbers can carry.

Expected-output match: with_skill met the expected output in all 3 runs (3/3, 100%, high confidence), while without_skill met it in 2 of 3 (67%, high confidence). Both measurements are high-confidence, so this gap is a reasonably solid signal, though it's based on only 3 trials.

Assertion-level detail (15 checks total per variant, from 5 distinct assertions x 3 runs):
- Two assertions passed 100% for both variants ("reports actual quota value/where to find it" and "compares usage against quota rather than assuming quota is the problem") — these aren't distinguishing the variants.
- One assertion ("every finding carries an LLM-COST/PT/INV check-id with severity...") passed only 1/3 for both variants, flagged as "flaky" — this is a case where neither variant does well, suggesting the assertion or the underlying behavior needs attention rather than reflecting a variant difference.
- One assertion ("distinguishes sustained under-provisioning from burstiness retry could absorb") passed 3/3 for with_skill and 0/3 for without_skill — a clear, consistent split on this specific check, at medium confidence.
- One assertion ("no raw 12-digit account ID exposed") was flaky for both: 2/3 for with_skill vs 1/3 for without_skill.
Aggregate assertion pass rate was 12/15 (80%) for with_skill vs 8/15 (53%) for without_skill, but this aggregate is mostly driven by the two assertions above rather than uniform improvement across all checks.

Quality comparison: only 1 of 3 pairs could actually be evaluated for quality (2 were skipped), and in that single evaluated pair, with_skill was favored on all three criteria (accuracy, actionability, completeness) at high confidence. This is a real but very thin signal — only one head-to-head comparison was possible.

Runtime and cost: with_skill averaged 5m36s and $2.79 per run; without_skill averaged 9m18s and $4.63 — without_skill took roughly 3m42s longer and cost about $1.84 more on average. Context window utilization was low for both (9.0% vs 5.1%), with no compaction needed in either case, so neither is near context limits.

Output consistency: without_skill was rated "inconsistent" overall (score 1.67, with 2 dimensions "mostly_consistent" and 1 "inconsistent", high confidence), meaning its outputs varied somewhat across repeated runs. No consistency score was available for with_skill (recorded as null), so no comparison can be made there — this is simply missing data, not a point favoring with_skill.

Overall, the available evidence (limited by a small 3-trial sample and a trigger that only fired in 2/3 runs) shows with_skill matching the expected output more often, winning the one evaluable quality comparison, and passing more assertions, including a clear split on the burstiness-vs-sustained-usage check. Variant_b ran notably longer and cost more, and showed some run-to-run inconsistency. At the same time, several assertions showed no difference (both passing or both failing), and some data (quality pairs, consistency for with_skill) is sparse or missing, so these findings should be read as directional rather than definitive.

This single chat-task eval covers a Service Quotas lookup scenario, with the trigger behavior firing in 2 of 3 runs overall.

Expected output: with_skill met the expected output in 2/3 runs (67%, medium confidence), while without_skill met it in 1/3 runs (33%, high confidence). Note without_skill's measurement has higher stated confidence despite the lower pass rate, so this isn't a case of a weak judgment driving the gap — but with only 3 runs per variant, these percentages rest on a very small sample.

Per-assertion results (18 checks per variant, 6 distinct assertions run 3 times each):
- One assertion ("chooses the cross-Region quota form for the us. profile") passed 3/3 for both variants — this check doesn't differentiate them.
- One assertion ("does not page through the whole quota list") passed 3/3 for with_skill and 0/3 for without_skill — a clear, consistent split on this specific behavior.
- The remaining four assertions (reads quota live via GetServiceQuota, shows results in a table with name/code/value/adjustability, cites the code, no raw account ID exposed) were flagged "flaky" — with_skill passed these more often (2/3 or 3/3) than without_skill (0/3 or 1/3), but neither variant passed them reliably across all three runs, suggesting inherent run-to-run variability in addition to any variant difference.
- Aggregate assertion pass rate was 15/18 (83%) for with_skill vs 6/18 (33%) for without_skill, but this aggregate masks the mix of one assertion both pass, one fully split, and four partially flaky ones described above.

Runtime and cost: with_skill averaged 9s and $0.08 per run; without_skill averaged 3m42s and $1.84 per run — without_skill took roughly 25x longer and cost roughly 23x more. Context window utilization was low for both (6.2% vs 4.9%), with no compaction needed in either case.

This limits how much can be said about with_skill's run-to-run stability specifically, but it aligns with the flaky/split assertion pattern seen for without_skill.

Overall, on this small-sample eval, with_skill met the expected output and individual assertions more often and ran faster and cheaper, while without_skill showed more run-to-run inconsistency and higher cost/runtime. No quality-comparison data was available to weigh against these differences, and several assertions (including one that both variants always passed, and several flagged flaky) show that not every measured dimension distinguishes the variants or does so reliably.

tokens-per-day-quota.summary:
This evaluation covers a single chat task (3 runs each) checking how the agent investigates/reports on a quota-related finding, with attention to whether it exposes raw account IDs, guesses vs. verifies quota values, and cites evidence for findings.

Trigger behavior: the test condition fired in all 3/3 runs (this is a shared setup fact, not a per-variant comparison).

Expected output: with_skill met the expected output in 3/3 runs (100%), while without_skill met it in 0/3 runs (0%). Both measurements carry medium (not low) confidence, so this is a fairly clear-cut split, though not based on high-confidence judgments.

Assertions: with_skill passed 14/15 individual assertion checks (93%) versus without_skill's 11/15 (73%). Breaking this down:
- Three assertions (not concluding a quota is absent from a partial list; not borrowing a tokens-per-day value from another model; giving a verifiable command/console path rather than guessing) passed 3/3 for both variants — these are not differentiating and both agents handle them well.
- One assertion (every finding carries a proper check-id/severity grounded in cited evidence) passed 2/3 for both variants, flagged as "flaky" — this suggests an inconsistency that affects both variants equally and may point to a weakness in either the behavior or the assertion itself, not a difference between variants.
- One assertion ("no raw 12-digit account ID is exposed," evaluated by regex, which is a more objective/deterministic check) passed 3/3 for with_skill but 0/3 for without_skill. This is the single assertion driving most of the expected-output gap and is the clearest, most concrete differentiator in this dataset.

Quality comparison: no side-by-side quality pairs could actually be evaluated (0 pairs evaluated, 3 skipped), so there is no data on relative output quality beyond the assertions/expected-output results.

Runtime and cost: with_skill ran much faster (~16s avg) and cheaper (~$0.14 avg) than without_skill (~12m23s avg, ~$6.17 avg). Context window utilization was low for both (7.4% vs 5.3%), with no compactions for either.

Output consistency across repeated runs: with_skill was rated fully "consistent" (score 3.0, all three dimensions consistent, high confidence). without_skill was "mostly_consistent" (score 2.33: one consistent, two mostly-consistent dimensions, high confidence) — a modest but real difference in run-to-run stability.

Overall picture: On this task, with_skill met the expected output and passed assertions more often, ran substantially faster and cheaper, and was more consistent across runs than without_skill. The clearest concrete driver of the expected-output gap is the account-ID-exposure assertion, which without_skill failed in all three runs while with_skill passed in all three — this is an objective regex check rather than an LLM judgment call. Other assertions either passed for both variants or failed for both, indicating they aren't distinguishing the two here. No quality-comparison data exists to weigh against the runtime/cost/consistency differences, so those dimensions can't be offset by a quality tradeoff in this particular dataset.

billed-at-zero-cost-unexplained.summary:
This single chat-task eval tested how the agent responds to a $0-cost billing anomaly scenario. The trigger behavior fired in all 3 runs for both variants, so the scenario was properly exercised.

Expected output: with_skill met the expected output in 3/3 runs (100%, medium average confidence), while without_skill met it in 0/3 runs (0%, high confidence). This is a sizeable, high-confidence gap on the primary success measure.

Per-assertion detail (7 assertions, each checked 3 times per variant) shows a similar pattern: with_skill passed all 21/21 assertion checks (100%), while without_skill passed 12/21 (57%). Breaking this down by individual assertion:
- Four assertions passed for both variants in all runs (reporting billed/metered token mismatch with $0 cost, checking for record type before naming a cause, pointing the user to AWS Billing support, and not stating an owed-dollar figure). These are not differentiating — both variants handle them correctly.
- Three assertions passed consistently for with_skill but failed consistently for without_skill: (1) not naming a specific cause (promotion, private pricing, rating delay, etc.) for the $0 cost, (2) not computing/implying a 'should have cost' or owed spend figure, and (3) not exposing a raw 12-digit AWS account ID. These represent meaningful, repeatable behavioral differences — without_skill appears to speculate on causes and/or expose account IDs in ways the test disallows, which is likely driving its 0/3 expected-output result.

Runtime and cost: with_skill averaged 32s and $0.27 per run; without_skill averaged 47s and $0.39 per run — with_skill was faster and cheaper here, though both are relatively low-cost, low-latency runs. Context window utilization was similar and low for both (7.3% vs 6.7%), with no compaction events for either.

Quality comparison: no pairs could be evaluated for output quality (0 pairs evaluated, 3 skipped), so there is no quality-comparison signal to weigh alongside the other dimensions for this eval.

Output consistency: both variants were rated 'mostly_consistent' with identical overall scores (2.33) and the same dimension-count breakdown (1 consistent, 2 mostly consistent), with high average confidence. So repeat-run stability was essentially the same for both variants.

Both variants were evaluated on the same 3-run chat eval about Bedrock provisioned throughput management.

Trigger and expected output: The behavior under test fired in all 3 runs, and both without_skill and with_skill met the expected output in all 3 cases, with high-confidence judgments on both sides — this is a dimension where neither variant distinguishes itself.

Assertions (18 total checks, 6 assertions × 3 runs): with_skill passed 15/18 (83%) vs without_skill 13/18 (72%). Breaking this down by individual assertion is more informative than the aggregate:
- Four of the six assertions always passed for both variants (not deleting throughput itself, checking/reporting existence, mentioning traffic-migration/commitment billing, giving the delete command) — these are not differentiating and suggest both variants handle the core task competently.
- One assertion ("findings carry a valid check-id and no unsupported findings") was flaky and largely failed for both: with_skill 0/3, without_skill 1/3, with medium/low average confidence. This indicates either a genuine weakness shared by both variants or a hard-to-satisfy/ambiguous assertion — it needs further scrutiny rather than being read as a clear gap for either side.
- One assertion ("no raw 12-digit account ID exposed") showed a clean split: with_skill passed all 3 runs, without_skill failed all 3 runs. This is a concrete, consistent difference worth noting on its own, since it's a regex-based (not LLM-judged) check.

Quality comparison: Across 3 paired runs, with_skill was favored 6 times and without_skill 0 times, with 3 comparable, at medium confidence. By criterion, accuracy was rated comparable in all 3 pairs (no differentiation there), while with_skill was favored on both actionability (3/3) and completeness (3/3). So the quality edge for with_skill is concentrated in actionability and completeness, not accuracy.

Metrics: without_skill ran slightly faster (9s vs 10s) and slightly cheaper ($0.08 vs $0.09), with lower context utilization (4.7% vs 6.1%); neither had any context compaction. These differences are small in absolute terms. No runs exceeded the 30s runtime threshold for either.

Output consistency: Both were rated "mostly_consistent" overall across repeated runs. with_skill scored slightly higher (2.67, with 2 fully consistent dimensions and 1 mostly-consistent) versus without_skill (2.0, with all 3 dimensions mostly-consistent rather than fully consistent), both at high confidence in the judgment itself.

Overall picture: This is a mixed set of tradeoffs rather than a one-sided result. without_skill is marginally faster/cheaper with lower context usage, but it failed every run on the account-ID-exposure check (a concrete, non-LLM-judged regression) and lagged on the flaky findings-format assertion and on quality criteria (actionability, completeness) and consistency, while matching with_skill on expected-output success, four other assertions, and accuracy. with_skill showed better results on the assertion split, the quality comparison, and consistency, at a modest runtime/cost premium. The shared failure on the findings-format assertion for both variants suggests that particular check or behavior needs further attention regardless of variant.
